stemBlocks.value: A square ABCD is drawn inside a circle with all four vertices on the circumference, and each side of the square is 11 cm. (i) Show that the diameter of the circle is 11√2 cm. (Only part (i) appears in this extract.)
Think first: The diagonal AC of the square passes through the centre of the circle, so the diagonal and the diameter are the same segment.

solutionSteps.instruction: Identify the right angle in the square.

solutionSteps.instruction: Apply Pythagoras' theorem to find the diagonal AC.
Take the square root and simplify the surd.
Explain why AC is a diameter.

contentBlocks.value: angle ABC = 90° stands on AC, and an angle in a semicircle is 90°, so AC passes through the centre

strategyBlocks.value: Apply Pythagoras to the right-angled triangle ABC formed by two sides and the diagonal, simplify the surd, and explain why that diagonal is a diameter.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) AC² = 11² + 11² = 242, so AC = √242 = 11√2 cm, and since angle ABC = 90° is subtended by AC the segment AC is a diameter. The diameter is therefore 11√2 cm.

whyThisWorks.value: In a square the diagonal makes a right-angled isosceles triangle with two sides, and Pythagoras gives its length as side x √2 every time. The diagonal is a diameter because the right angle at B stands on AC, and the converse of the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem says a chord subtending a right angle on the circle must pass through the centre. Both diagonals of the square are therefore diameters, which is also why the centre of the circle is the centre of the square.
